questions.q: Bromobenzene and bromoethane are treated with sodium in dry ether. The main product is:
questions.explain: In the Wurtz–Fittig reaction the aryl and alkyl groups join where the halogens were: C₆H₅Br + C₂H₅Br + 2Na → C₆H₅C₂H₅ + 2NaBr. Biphenyl and butane are only the self-coupled side products.

questions.q: Which compound is NOT formed when bromobenzene and bromomethane react with sodium in dry ether?
questions.explain: Three couplings occur: Ar–R (toluene, main), R–R (ethane, Wurtz) and Ar–Ar (biphenyl, Fittig). Ethylbenzene would need an ethyl group, which neither halide supplies.

questions.q: In the organosodium picture of the Wurtz–Fittig reaction, the cross product Ar–R is favoured because:
options: The alkyl halide reacts with sodium faster and forms R⁻Na⁺, which then attacks the aryl halide
The aryl halide forms an aryl carbocation that the alkyl halide attacks
Sodium reacts only with aryl halides
Dry ether reacts with the aryl halide first
questions.explain: Alkyl halides are more reactive towards sodium than aryl halides (Wurtz > Fittig), so R⁻Na⁺ forms first and displaces X⁻ from Ar–X. Pairing halogens from different periods, such as ArCl with RBr, widens this difference.

questions.q: Which aryl halide is unsuitable as a substrate for the Wurtz–Fittig reaction?
questions.explain: Ring groups that react with sodium, such as OH, NO₂, C=O and COOH, are not tolerated, so the phenolic OH rules out 4-bromophenol. A methyl group on the ring does not react with sodium.
